title: Binary codes beyond the Gilbert–Varshamov bound
formal:
Do binary error-correcting codes have an asymptotic rate strictly above the Gilbert–Varshamov bound at some fixed positive relative Hamming distance?

Precisely, do there exist real constants \(0<\delta<1/2\) and \(\eta>0\) such that for every integer \(N\ge1\) there are an integer \(n\ge N\) and a nonempty code \(C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) satisfying
\[\forall x,y\in C,\quad x\ne y\ \Longrightarrow\ d_H(x,y)\ge\lceil\delta n\rceil,\]
\[\frac{\log_2|C|}{n}\ \ge\ 1-H_2(\delta)+\eta?\]
The constants precede the block length and code. Codes may be nonlinear, and neither an efficient construction nor an efficient decoder is required.
definitions:
A binary word of block length \(n\) is a function from \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) to \(\{0,1\}\). Its Hamming distance from another word is
\[d_H(x,y)=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\ne y_i\}|.\]
A code is a nonempty subset of this finite set of words, with distinct elements counted once. The pairwise distance condition is vacuous for a singleton, which has rate zero and cannot meet the stated positive-rate target. The ceiling \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\) is the least integer at least \(\delta n\); using the real threshold \(\delta n\) is equivalent because distance is integral.

The rate of \(C\) is \(\log_2|C|/n\), measured in information bits per transmitted binary symbol. No assumption that \(|C|\) is a power of two is made. The binary entropy function is
\[H_2(t)=-t\log_2 t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\quad(0<t<1),\]
with endpoint values \(H_2(0)=H_2(1)=0\). All logarithms in the statement are base two. The comparison \(1-H_2(\delta)\) is the binary Gilbert–Varshamov asymptotic rate benchmark at relative minimum distance \(\delta\).

For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le d\le n\), define
\[A_2(n,d)=\max\{|C|:\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ d_H(x,y)\ge d\text{ for all distinct }x,y\in C\}.\]
The maximum exists because the cube is finite. Equivalently, the target asks whether
\[\exists\delta\in(0,1/2):\quad R_2^*(\delta)>1-H_2(\delta),\qquad R_2^*(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)}{n}.\]
Here the limit superior of the bounded sequence \(a_n\) means \(\inf_{N\ge1}\sup_{n\ge N}a_n\). An unbounded sequence of successful lengths suffices; codes need not be supplied at every length. The additive improvement \(\eta\) must remain a fixed positive constant. Letting the distance fraction or the improvement depend on \(n\) does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.

This is an existence problem over ordinary finite subsets, with no time, space, randomness, encoding or decoding constraint. A linear binary code, meaning a vector subspace over the two-element field, is allowed but not required. Error distance concerns coordinate substitutions; insertions, deletions, erasures and quantum errors define other tasks. The target is a pairwise minimum-distance condition, not a list-decoding radius or the capacity of a channel with independently random errors.

context_blocks.text: The Gilbert–Varshamov theorem supplies binary codes with asymptotic rate at least \(1-H_2(\delta)\). It is a lower bound on what is achievable, not an upper bound on all codes. The question is whether a fixed distance fraction admits a strictly larger asymptotic rate. The textbook lists determination of the optimal tradeoff as a central unresolved question.

Minimum distance and correctable error fraction are different parameters. Pairwise distance at least \(d\) makes unique recovery information-theoretically possible after any \(\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor\) substitutions. Thus distance fraction \(\delta\) corresponds asymptotically to fewer than \(\delta/2\) adversarial substitutions per symbol, not \(\delta\). The entropy formula for an independently noisy binary channel describes a different probability model.

An additive rate gain \(\eta\) means at least \(2^{\eta n}\) times as many codewords as the exponential benchmark \(2^{n(1-H_2(\delta))}\). Multiplying the number of codewords by \(n^c\), for any fixed \(c\), adds only \(c\log_2 n/n\) to the rate. That gain vanishes as the block length grows. This distinction explains why a paper can improve the Gilbert–Varshamov code-size bound without settling this card.

Jiang and Vardy prove a larger finite-length lower bound. Write \(V(n,r)=\sum_{i=0}^r\binom ni\) for the size of a Hamming ball. Their Theorem 2 improves the elementary count \(2^n/V(n,d-1)\) by a factor proportional to \(\log_2 V(n,d-1)\), in its stated distance range. For fixed positive distance fraction below 0.499, this factor has order \(n\), so its extra normalized rate tends to zero. The paper explicitly says that asymptotic tightness in rate could still hold.

The existence question also differs from explicit construction. The 2025 textbook gives these separate open-question entries: codes might attain or exceed a rate nonconstructively even if no efficient description, encoder or decoder is known. Conversely, making an existing rate explicit does not improve the existential rate. The present target imposes none of those computational requirements.

Algebraic-geometric codes over some larger finite alphabets already exceed the corresponding Gilbert–Varshamov benchmark. This does not by itself supply binary codes exceeding the binary benchmark: changing alphabets changes both the rate normalization and distance parameters. The July 2026 trace-code paper concerns conversion toward explicit high-distance binary codes, and its abstract explicitly reports no improved construction. Its analysis-specific limitations should not be read as an impossibility theorem for arbitrary binary codes.

The November 2025 small-bias-set report gives further progress on explicit binary constructions near the high-distance Gilbert–Varshamov scale. The inspected abstract concerns achieving that scale explicitly. It does not claim a fixed positive rate improvement above the existential bound. Its full proof was not audited in this review.

The January 2026 hierarchy paper studies stronger linear-programming relaxations for linear codes. Its completeness theorem becomes exact when the hierarchy level is at least the block length. That is different from deriving a new asymptotic upper bound at a fixed level, and the theorem’s linear-code scope is narrower than the universal class in this card. Neither feature resolves the nonlinear rate-distance question.

The paper published on 9 September 2026 gives another proof of the first linear-programming upper bound, \(R_2^*(\delta)\le H_2(1/2-\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)})\). It explicitly obtains the same asymptotic bound as earlier work. This is not the strongest known upper bound throughout the interval: the second MRRW bound is stronger in part of the range. The inspected introduction still identifies the optimal binary rate as unknown, with a gap above the Gilbert–Varshamov lower bound.

The recent arXiv check also found an 11 September 2026 revision of the deletion-code paper first submitted in 2022. Its logarithmic improvement is for a fixed number of deletions, whose distance is governed by common subsequences. Both that error model and that asymptotic regime differ from a fixed fraction of Hamming substitutions. Its title and revision date therefore do not constitute a resolution of this card.

why: A binary code trades the amount of information stored in each symbol against the number of adversarial substitutions that can be tolerated. This question asks whether the ubiquitous random-coding rate is an actual information limit or whether binary codebooks can carry a fixed additional amount of information per symbol at the same relative distance. It concerns what codes can exist, independently of implementation efficiency.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed existence proposition or its full logical negation. A positive answer must establish fixed constants \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), \(\eta>0\) and suitable binary codes for unbounded lengths, with the stated distance and rate. A negative answer must show that for every such \(\delta\) and every \(\eta>0\), some integer \(N\ge1\) satisfies: every \(n\ge N\) and every eligible binary code of distance at least \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\) has rate strictly less than \(1-H_2(\delta)+\eta\). The universal upper bound must cover nonlinear codes as well as linear ones. A finite-length gain, a gain tending to zero in normalized rate, or a result for a different alphabet or error metric does not establish the positive answer. No algorithmic efficiency is required.

progress.text: Jiang and Vardy improve binary code size by a factor of order the block length at fixed distance fraction in the stated range; the normalized-rate gain vanishes.
The textbook distinguishes the still-open optimal binary rate-distance tradeoff from explicit construction at the Gilbert–Varshamov bound.
An ECCC report advances explicit small-bias sets near the high-distance GV scale.
Higher-order LP results establish completeness for linear codes at levels growing to the block length.
The ICALP trace-code paper improves structural analysis without claiming an improved binary-code construction.
A newly published proof recovers the first LP upper bound and does not close the asymptotic rate gap.
A new revision of the deletion-code paper concerns a different metric and a fixed-number-error regime.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected 2025 textbook and September 2026 first-LP paper retain the asymptotic binary rate-distance gap. Jiang–Vardy improve code size without a constant normalized-rate gain. The 2026 linear-code hierarchy and trace-code papers do not resolve the unrestricted target; the recent deletion-code revision concerns another metric. No matching resolution was found in the bounded search. Abstract-only checks and their limits are recorded in the review.

source_formulation.text: Preserves importance 96 and the existing existential constant-gap binary Hamming-distance target, allowing arbitrary nonlinear codes and an unbounded subsequence of block lengths. The coding textbook separates the optimal asymptotic rate-distance question from explicit construction at the Gilbert–Varshamov bound. The equivalent limit-superior formulation makes that distinction precise without replacing the target by the entire optimal curve.

sentences: Binary error-correcting codes store information in words whose pairwise Hamming distances are large.
The Gilbert–Varshamov bound guarantees a familiar asymptotic rate at each fixed relative distance.
This question asks whether some fixed distance permits a fixed positive rate improvement for unbounded block lengths.
Codes may be nonlinear and need not have an efficient construction or decoding algorithm.
Known finite-length gains and recent explicit-construction or upper-bound papers do not settle that constant-gap existence question.
